name: Kwame Nkrumah
info: Kwame Nkrumah was a Ghanaian politician and Pan-Africanist who led the Gold Coast to independence as Ghana in 1957, the first in sub-Saharan Africa, and ruled it, latterly as a one-party state, until a coup in 1966.

facts.born: 21 September 1909 by his own account (his mother later gave 1912), at Nkroful in the Nzema area of the Gold Coast; son of a goldsmith, Opanyin Kofi Nwiana Ngolomah, of the Asona clan, and Elizabeth Nyanibah, a fishmonger and petty trader
facts.died: 27 April 1972, in Bucharest, of an unknown but apparently incurable sickness, after six years of exile in Conakry, Guinea
facts.role: General secretary of the United Gold Coast Convention (1947); founder and leader of the Convention People's Party (1949); Leader of Government Business (1951) and Prime Minister of the Gold Coast (1952-1957); Prime Minister of Ghana (1957-1960); President of Ghana (1960-1966), from 1964 president for life of a one-party state
facts.known: Leading Ghana to independence in 1957; the Convention People's Party and Positive Action; Pan-Africanism and the founding of the Organisation of African Unity; the Volta River Project and the Akosombo Dam; expansion of schooling; the Preventive Detention Act and the one-party state; the 1966 coup

t: After twelve years of study and organising in the United States and Britain, Nkrumah returned to the Gold Coast in 1947 and built the Convention People's Party, whose landslide in 1951 brought him from prison to the head of government.
He led Ghana to independence in 1957 and made it a centre of Pan-Africanism and the decolonisation of Africa, while spending heavily on roads, harbours, schools and the Akosombo Dam.

His rule grew authoritarian, with detention without trial, a press under state control and, from 1964, a one-party state with himself as president for life, until the military and police overthrew him in 1966.
dyk: While studying at the University of Pennsylvania, Nkrumah worked with the linguist William Everett Welmers, providing the spoken material on which the first descriptive grammar of his native Fante dialect of the Akan language was based.
ev: Kwame Nkrumah is born at Nkroful in the Gold Coast
He founds the Convention People's Party
The party wins the Gold Coast election in a landslide and he is released from prison to form a government
The Gold Coast becomes independent as Ghana, with Nkrumah as prime minister
Ghana becomes a republic and Nkrumah is elected its president
A constitutional amendment makes Ghana a one-party state with Nkrumah as president for life
He is overthrown in a coup while on a state visit to China
Nkrumah dies in Bucharest, after years of exile in Guinea

sections.early:
Kwame Nkrumah was born, by his own account, on 21 September 1909 at Nkroful, a small village in the Nzema area of the south-west Gold Coast near the border with the French Ivory Coast; his mother later gave the year as 1912. He was his mother's only child. His father, Opanyin Kofi Nwiana Ngolomah, a goldsmith of the Asona clan of the Akan, had several wives; his mother, Elizabeth Nyanibah, was a fishmonger and petty trader. At three he moved with his mother to Half Assini, where he went to a Catholic mission school, completed its ten-year course in eight years and in 1925 was baptised a Catholic.

The Reverend Alec Garden Fraser brought him to train as a teacher at the Government Training College, soon Achimota School, in Accra. There the deputy headmaster Kwegyir Aggrey introduced him to the ideas of Marcus Garvey and W. E. B. Du Bois, and Nkrumah came to believe, echoing Garvey, that only when the black race governed itself could there be harmony between the races. After gaining his teacher's certificate in 1930 he taught at Elmina and Axim and at the seminary at Amissano, and considered becoming a Jesuit. He had heard the journalist Nnamdi Azikiwe speak, and Azikiwe's influence increased his interest in black nationalism; on Azikiwe's advice he set out, with money from relatives, for Lincoln University in Pennsylvania. On the way, in Britain, he learned to his outrage of Italy's invasion of Ethiopia. He reached the United States in October 1935.
sections.rise:
In America he earned degrees at Lincoln and the University of Pennsylvania, worked menial jobs, spent summers among the street orators of Harlem and organised the African Students Association of America and Canada, urging a Pan-African strategy. In May 1945 he went to London, where with George Padmore he was a principal organiser of the Fifth Pan-African Congress in Manchester that October and became secretary of the West African National Secretariat.

In 1947 the United Gold Coast Convention (UGCC) hired him as its general secretary, and he returned home in November. After the Accra riots of February 1948 the colonial government arrested six UGCC leaders, among them Nkrumah and J. B. Danquah. Freed in April, he founded the Accra Evening News and a youth wing whose motto was "Self-Government Now", and on 12 June 1949 he broke away to form the Convention People's Party (CPP). Its vans, music and red cockerel reached ordinary voters as earlier politics, aimed at the urban intelligentsia, had not. In January 1950 he called for "positive action"; a general strike turned violent and he was sentenced to three years in prison. In the election of February 1951, the first under universal franchise in colonial Africa, the CPP won 34 of the 38 seats contested by parties, with Nkrumah elected from prison. The governor, Charles Arden-Clarke, released him on 12 February and asked him to form a government.
sections.deeds:
As Leader of Government Business and, from 1952, prime minister, Nkrumah spent the colony's cocoa reserves on a five-year development plan: trunk roads, modernised railways, water and sewer systems, a new harbour at Tema and new schools, which raised the number of pupils from 200,000 in 1951 to 500,000 in 1956. Against the National Liberation Movement, which wanted a federal state, he held to a unitary constitution, and after the election of July 1956 the assembly voted for independence under the name he had proposed, Ghana. On 6 March 1957 Ghana became the first of Britain's African colonies to gain majority-rule independence, and Nkrumah proclaimed, "Ghana will be free forever."

His government introduced free health care and education, made primary schooling compulsory in 1962 and set up a minimum wage and social security. The centrepiece of his economic programme was the Volta River Project, the Akosombo Dam, which he opened on 22 January 1966. In 1960 Ghana became a republic with Nkrumah as president.

Abroad he made Ghana a leader of the Pan-African movement, hosting the First Conference of Independent States and the All-African Peoples' Conference in 1958 and forming a Union of African States with Guinea and Mali in 1960. He sent more than a thousand troops to the United Nations force in the Congo, was a founding member of the Non-Aligned Movement in 1961 and was instrumental in creating the Organisation of African Unity in 1963. In 1962 the Soviet Union awarded him the Lenin Peace Prize.
sections.opponents:
Unrest came soon after independence. Nkrumah banned regional and tribal parties in 1957, had chiefs who opposed the CPP destooled, and in 1958, convinced that there had been a plot to kill him, had parliament pass the Preventive Detention Act, allowing imprisonment for up to five years without charge or trial. His biographer David Birmingham judges that "no single measure did more to bring down Nkrumah's reputation". When three CPP members accused of plotting to bomb his motorcade in 1962 were acquitted, he sacked the chief judge and had them retried and sentenced to death, later commuted; the president was then given power to remove judges. From 1960 he claimed the right of pre-publication censorship of all news. The 1964 amendment making the CPP the only legal party passed with 99.91 percent of the vote, which observers condemned as "obviously rigged".

His opponents included Kofi Abrefa Busia of the United Party, who called the ban on tribal politics repressive, and the chiefs, whose powers his laws curtailed and who came to look favourably on his overthrow. Cocoa farmers, a constituency that had brought him to power, were alienated when he took their windfall through levies and raised their taxes to service the debt for the dam. He fostered a cult of personality, took the title Osagyefo, "redeemer", and put his image on stamps and money. Edward Luttwak argued that his mismanagement of the economy was considerable but that he was undone by the very success of development, which educated critics he could not repress.
sections.last:
In February 1966, while Nkrumah was on a state visit to China on the way to North Vietnam and North Korea, the military and police, with backing from the civil service, overthrew his government in a violent coup. The conspirators, led by Joseph Arthur Ankrah, called themselves the National Liberation Council and ruled as a military government for three years. Nkrumah learned of the coup only on arriving in China, where Zhou Enlai received him with courtesy for four days.

He then went to live in Conakry, the capital of Guinea, where he was named honorary co-president and lay low. In his memoir Dark Days in Ghana he alluded to American involvement in the coup, perhaps on the basis of documents shown to him by the KGB. In 1978 John Stockwell, a former CIA officer turned critic, wrote that the CIA's Accra station had kept intimate contact with the plotters, and Seymour Hersh defended his account; these claims have never been verified.

After the coup Ghana cut its ties with Guinea and the Eastern Bloc, turned to the West and invited the International Monetary Fund and World Bank to take a leading role in its economy, losing stature among African nationalists. Nkrumah died in Bucharest, the capital of Romania, on 27 April 1972, of an unknown but apparently incurable sickness. His wife, Fathia Ritzk, an Egyptian Coptic bank worker whom he had married on the evening of her arrival in Ghana, had borne him three children: Gamal, Samia and Sekou.
sections.legacy:
Nkrumah is remembered above all as the leader of the first black African colony to shake off colonial rule; listeners to the BBC World Service voted him African of the millennium, and the BBC described him as a "Hero of Independence". His greatest success as a Pan-Africanist was his influence on the founding of the Organisation of African Unity. Inspired by Garvey, Du Bois and Padmore, he championed the "African Personality" and "Africa for the Africans", and drew Du Bois and Kwame Ture, among others, to settle in Ghana. In the United States he became a symbol of black liberation; Ralph Bunche told him in 1958 that he was "a true and living representation of our hopes and ideals".

His writings, among them Africa Must Unite and Neo-Colonialism, the Last Stage of Imperialism, set out a non-aligned Marxist view: capitalism's effects would long burden Africa, and a scientific socialism grounded in the egalitarianism of traditional African society would answer them. A State Department document records that he "was doing more to undermine [U.S. government] interests than any other black African".

In Ghana, 21 September, the centenary of his birth, was declared Founders' Day in 2009 and renamed Kwame Nkrumah Memorial Day in 2019. The Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology and the Kwame Nkrumah Memorial Park and Mausoleum in Accra bear his name, and an annual "Journey to Nkroful" marks his birthday.

summary: Kwame Nkrumah, born in the Gold Coast in 1909, studied in the United States and Britain, founded the Convention People's Party and in 1957 led Ghana to independence, the first in sub-Saharan Africa. A leading Pan-Africanist, he ruled through detention without trial and a one-party state until a coup in 1966, and died in exile in 1972.
